prompt.en: The scientist, along with her assistants, ______ preparing to publish the findings next month.
prompt.mn: Эрдэмтэн туслахуудынхаа хамт ирэх сард үр дүнгээ нийтлэхээр бэлтгэж байна. Хоосон зайд тохирох үйл үгийг сонго.

options.mn: have been — олон тооны төгс цаг

explanation.en: Review the source text and the correct answer.
explanation.mn: Эзэн бие нь ганц тооны “The scientist”; “along with her assistants” нь тоог өөрчлөхгүй. Ганц тооны “is” зөв.

prompt.en: Choose the word that best completes the text: The ancient manuscript was so ______ that scholars could barely decipher a single line.

explanation.en: Review the source text and the correct answer.
explanation.mn: “scarcely decipher” = уншихад бэрх, тиймээс “illegible” (уншигдахгүй) зөв. Legible нь эсрэг утга.

prompt.en: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition? “The bridge was structurally sound. ______, engineers recommended closing it for cosmetic repairs.”
prompt.mn: Гүүрийн бүтэц бат бөх байв. ______, инженерүүд өнгө үзэмжийн засварт хаахыг зөвлөжээ. Утгыг зөв холбох үгийг сонго.

explanation.en: Review the source text and the correct answer.
explanation.mn: Бат бөх атлаа хаах санал — эсрэгцэл. “Nonetheless” (гэсэн ч) зөв.

prompt.en: The novelist’s early works, ______ received little attention, are now regarded as masterpieces.
prompt.mn: Зохиолчийн анхны бүтээлүүд тухайн үедээ анхаарал бага татсан ч одоо шилдэг бүтээлд тооцогддог. Бүтээлийг тодотгох зөв төлөөний үгийг сонго.

explanation.en: Review the source text and the correct answer.
explanation.mn: Эд юмс (“works”)-ыг тодотгож байгаа тул “which” зөв; “who/whom” хүнд хэрэглэнэ.

prompt.en: Based on the text, the author’s primary purpose is to ______ (passage: a review praising a documentary’s cinematography while criticizing its pacing).
prompt.mn: Баримтат киноны зураг авалтыг магтсан ч өрнөлийн хэмнэлийг шүүмжилсэн тоймын гол зорилго юу вэ?

prompt.en: Select the choice that conforms to Standard English: “Each of the students ______ responsible for their own materials.”

prompt.en: The committee will announce the winners; ______, the ceremony will be held online this year.

prompt.en: Which choice best maintains parallel structure? “The workshop taught participants to code, to design, and ______.”

preparation, the — англи цэг тэмдэг, бүтцийг харьцуул

questions.passage:
Bringing Back the Wetlands
For much of the twentieth century, wetlands were regarded as wasteland. Marshes and
bogs were drained on a vast scale to create farmland, control mosquitoes or make room for
expanding towns. It is estimated that more than half of the world's wetlands disappeared
during  this  period.  Attitudes  shifted  only  in  recent  decades,  once  scientists  began  to
measure how much these waterlogged landscapes actually do for us.
Wetlands function as natural infrastructure. They act as sponges, absorbing heavy rainfall
and  releasing  it  slowly,  which  reduces  the  severity  of  floods  downstream.  They  filter
pollutants from water, trapping sediments and breaking down contaminants before they
reach rivers and reservoirs. Peat-forming wetlands also store large quantities of carbon,
more per hectare than forests, which makes their protection valuable in limiting climate
change.
Recognising  this,  governments  and  conservation  groups  have  increasingly  turned  to
wetland restoration. The approach varies. In some cases it is as simple as blocking the
drainage ditches that once dried the land, allowing water to return naturally. In others, it
involves reintroducing native plants or even reshaping the terrain. Restored wetlands can
recover surprisingly quickly, with birds, amphibians and insects returning within a few
seasons.
Restoration is not without difficulties, however. Land that has been farmed for generations
is often privately owned, and persuading owners to give it up can be costly and slow. There
is also debate over how to measure success: a site may look healthy yet fail to deliver the
carbon  storage  or  biodiversity  that  was  hoped  for.  Critics  caution  against  treating
restoration as a simple offset that licenses continued destruction elsewhere.
Despite these reservations, momentum is growing. Several countries have set targets to
restore wetlands over the coming decade, and early results are encouraging. Land once
dismissed as useless swamp is now treated as a resource worth protecting.

questions.passage:
The Quiet Rise of the E-Reader
When electronic reading devices first appeared, many predicted the swift extinction of the
printed book. Two decades later, the outcome has been mixed. E-readers did capture a
substantial share of the market, particularly for genre fiction that readers consume quickly
and  rarely  keep.  Yet  printed  books  have  shown  remarkable  resilience,  and  in  several
countries their sales have even edged upwards after years of decline.
Part of the explanation lies in what researchers call the "physicality" of print. Studies
suggest that readers often remember information better when they read it on paper,
possibly because the fixed layout of a physical page gives the brain spatial cues to anchor
memories. Others simply value the tactile pleasure of a book: its weight, the smell of the
paper, and the sense of progress as pages accumulate on the left.
E-readers, for their part, offer undeniable practical advantages. A single lightweight device
can store thousands of titles, adjust font size for tired eyes, and deliver a new book within
seconds. For travellers and students, this convenience is transformative. The devices have
also opened up reading to people with visual impairments, thanks to adjustable text and
built-in dictionaries.
Rather than one format replacing the other, the two now coexist, each suited to different
situations. Many readers switch between them, using an e-reader on a crowded commute
and a printed book at home. The printed book has not disappeared in the way some once
predicted.

questions.passage:
Why We Sleep the Way We Do
Sleep can feel like wasted time, hours in which nothing is achieved. Yet research over
recent decades has shown it to be one of the most active and essential periods of our
lives. Rather than shutting down, the sleeping brain consolidates memories, clears waste
products and repairs tissue. Deprive a person of sleep for long enough and almost every
system in the body begins to falter.
Human sleep is organised into cycles, each lasting roughly ninety minutes and moving
through  distinct  stages.  The  deepest  stages  are  thought  to  be  crucial  for  physical
restoration, while the stage known as REM, in which most vivid dreaming occurs, appears
to play a role in emotional processing and creativity. A full night allows several complete
cycles, which is why fragmented or shortened sleep can leave us feeling unrefreshed even
after many hours in bed.
Modern life, however, is remarkably hostile to good sleep. Artificial light, and particularly
the blue light emitted by screens, can suppress melatonin, the hormone that signals the
body  to  wind  down.  Irregular  schedules,  caffeine  and  the  pressure  to  be  constantly
available all conspire against the steady rhythm our bodies evolved to follow. The result,
researchers warn, is a widespread and chronic sleep debt.
The good news is that many of the remedies are simple. Keeping a consistent bedtime,
dimming lights in the evening and avoiding screens before bed can all make a measurable
difference. Sleep is not a luxury to be sacrificed but a foundation for health, mood and
memory.

questions.passage:
Why We Sleep the Way We Do
Sleep can feel like wasted time, hours in which nothing is achieved. Yet research over
recent decades has shown it to be one of the most active and essential periods of our
lives. Rather than shutting down, the sleeping brain consolidates memories, clears waste
products and repairs tissue. Deprive a person of sleep for long enough and almost every
system in the body begins to falter.
Human sleep is organised into cycles, each lasting roughly ninety minutes and moving
through  distinct  stages.  The  deepest  stages  are  thought  to  be  crucial  for  physical
restoration, while the stage known as REM, in which most vivid dreaming occurs, appears
to play a role in emotional processing and creativity. A full night allows several complete
cycles, which is why fragmented or shortened sleep can leave us feeling unrefreshed even
after many hours in bed.
Modern life, however, is remarkably hostile to good sleep. Artificial light, and particularly
the blue light emitted by screens, can suppress melatonin, the hormone that signals the
body  to  wind  down.  Irregular  schedules,  caffeine  and  the  pressure  to  be  constantly
available all conspire against the steady rhythm our bodies evolved to follow. The result,
researchers warn, is a widespread and chronic sleep debt.
The good news is that many of the remedies are simple. Keeping a consistent bedtime,
dimming lights in the evening and avoiding screens before bed can all make a measurable
difference. Sleep is not a luxury to be sacrificed but a foundation for health, mood and
memory.

questions.passage:
The Economics of the Coffee Shop
The independent coffee shop has become a familiar feature of towns across the world, yet
running one is a far more precarious business than its relaxed atmosphere suggests.
Margins on a single cup of coffee are thin once rent, wages, equipment and the beans
themselves are accounted for. To survive, most owners rely not on any single sale but on
volume, loyalty and the careful management of costs that customers never see.
Location is often the decisive factor. A shop on a busy street may pay several times the
rent of one tucked away on a quieter road, but the additional footfall can more than justify
the expense. Get the calculation wrong, however, and high rent quickly becomes a fatal
burden. Many promising cafés have closed not because their coffee was poor but because
they simply could not sell enough of it to cover the cost of their prime address.
Owners have responded with ingenuity. Some extend their hours into the evening, serving
food and drinks to spread fixed costs across more of the day. Others build a sense of
community by hosting events, learning regulars' names and creating a space people return
to for reasons that have little to do with the drink itself. This loyalty, economists note, is
one of the few defences a small café has against the buying power of large chains.
The economics of the coffee shop comes down to small margins and steady relationships.
Success rarely depends on a single clever idea. It depends on doing many ordinary things
well at the same time: controlling waste, choosing the right site and treating customers
well.

The independent coffee shop has become a familiar feature of towns across the world, yet
running one is a far more precarious business than its relaxed atmosphere suggests.
Margins on a single cup of coffee are thin once rent, wages, equipment and the beans
themselves are accounted for. To survive, most owners rely not on any single sale but on
volume, loyalty and the careful management of costs that customers never see.
Location is often the decisive factor. A shop on a busy street may pay several times the
rent of one tucked away on a quieter road, but the additional footfall can more than justify
the expense. Get the calculation wrong, however, and high rent quickly becomes a fatal
burden. Many promising cafés have closed not because their coffee was poor but because
they simply could not sell enough of it to cover the cost of their prime address.

community by hosting events, learning regulars' names and creating a space people return
to for reasons that have little to do with the drink itself. This loyalty, economists note, is
one of the few defences a small café has against the buying power of large chains.

Dogs were the first animals humans ever domesticated, long before cattle, sheep, or
crops. Genetic evidence suggests that dogs descended from wolves at least 15,000 years
ago, though the exact time and place remain debated. One popular theory holds that
domestication began not because humans captured wolves, but because certain wolves
began to approach human camps in search of food scraps. The tamer, less fearful wolves
were more successful at getting food and gradually grew closer to humans over many
generations. In time, this partnership benefited both species: dogs gained a reliable food
source and protection, while humans gained help with hunting, herding, and guarding.
This long relationship may explain why dogs are unusually skilled at reading human
gestures and emotions — a talent few other animals share.
